source.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning

accepted.question_text: In fully decentralized federated learning for deep neural networks, can stochastic gradient methods be made robust to realistic client unreliability—clients temporarily disappearing, joining late, or dropping messages—without relying on a central server, while still converging under the communication delays and asynchrony imposed by the network topology?

evidence.quote: for the case of deep learning and SGD this remains an open question.

accepted.question_text: For fully decentralized learning with non-identically distributed client data and multiple local update steps between communications, what convergence guarantees are achievable, and what model-averaging policy yields the fastest convergence without sacrificing practicality?

evidence.quote: understanding the convergence under non-IID data distributions and how to design a model averaging policy that achieves the fastest convergence remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: How can fully decentralized federated learning be realized in practice, and what minimal form of trusted central authority, if any, is still required to define the learning task, choose the algorithm and hyperparameters, and coordinate debugging or governance?

evidence.quote: open problems are in practical realization of the idea and in understanding of what form of trusted central authority is needed to set up the task.

accepted.question_text: What kinds of cross-client statistical heterogeneity actually occur in real federated datasets, and how can those empirical patterns be characterized well enough to build realistic benchmark datasets and mitigation strategies for different non-IID regimes?

evidence.quote: the characterization of cross-client differences in real-world partitioned datasets is an important open question.

accepted.question_text: How should methods for handling dataset shift be adapted to federated learning, where the distribution of eligible clients and the relation between the training population and the deployment population can change over time?

evidence.quote: Adapting techniques for handling dataset shift to federated learning is another interesting open question.

accepted.question_text: In the independent-and-identically-distributed setting, can federated averaging or closely related local-update methods be improved so that they match the accelerated convergence rate known for mini-batch stochastic gradient descent under intermittent communication constraints?

evidence.quote: It is an open problem if federated averaging algorithms can close this gap.

accepted.question_text: For federated optimization on heterogeneous client data, in which regimes do taking more than one local optimization step per communication round help convergence, and in which regimes do they instead slow or destabilize learning?

evidence.quote: Clarifying the regimes where K > 1 may hurt or help convergence is an important open problem.

accepted.question_text: How can federated models be designed to use user-specific and context-specific features—such as a user’s frequent words, the app being used, or conversational context—so that a single shared model still produces highly personalized predictions without requiring per-user fine-tuning?

evidence.quote: developing model architectures that can effectively incorporate context information for different tasks remains an important open problem with the potential to greatly increase the utility of FL-trained models.

accepted.question_text: Can federated learning support intermediate points between one global model and one model per client by learning task-specific or cluster-specific submodels over subsets of clients, while remaining practical in cross-device settings?

evidence.quote: The development of such algorithms is an important open problem.

accepted.question_text: Under what assumptions do meta-learning-based personalization methods such as MAML-style approaches work well in federated learning, and what metrics should be used to evaluate personalized performance fairly across clients rather than only global accuracy?

evidence.quote: it would be useful to analyze the theoretical guarantees of MAML-type techniques and study under what assumptions they can be successful

none of the existing works clearly formulates what would be comprehensive metrics for measuring personalized performance; for instance, is a small improvement for every client preferable to a larger improvement for a subset of clients?

accepted.question_text: Under what conditions is a single global model learned by federated learning more accurate on a client than a model trained only on that client’s local data, and can one design personalization methods with theoretical guarantees that match or beat both baselines?

evidence.quote: a natural theoretical question is to determine under what conditions the shared global model is better than independent per-device models.

Can we guarantee that the model hFL learned via federated learning is at least as accurate as hk when used for client k? Can we quantify how much improvement can be expected via federated leaning? And can we develop personalization strategies with theoretical guarantees that at least match the performance of both natural baselines (hk and hFL)?

accepted.question_text: How can hyperparameter optimization for federated learning be made communication-efficient and computationally feasible on resource-constrained devices, and can federated optimizers be made robust enough to require little manual tuning across tasks and architectures?

evidence.quote: further research should consider developing solutions for efficient hyperparameter optimization in the context of federated learning.
the development of easy-to-tune optimization algorithms is a major open area.

accepted.question_text: What privacy-preserving techniques can support debugging, interpretability, data inspection, and bias analysis in federated learning when the raw decentralized data cannot be directly examined, and how can differentially private generative models for this purpose be made more faithful?

evidence.quote: Developing privacy-preserving techniques to answer such questions on decentralized data is a major open problem.
the development of algorithms that improve the fidelity of FL DP generative models.

accepted.question_text: What are the fundamental trade-offs between communication cost and learning accuracy in federated learning, and can one jointly design gradient compression, model broadcast compression, and local computation reduction methods that are simultaneously efficient, compatible with secure aggregation, and compatible with differential privacy?

evidence.quote: Joint design of compression methods that are compatible with Secure Aggregation, or for which differential privacy guarantees can be obtained, is thus a valuable open problem.

it remains unclear if communication cost can be further reduced, and whether any of these methods or their combinations can come close to providing optimal trade-offs between communication and accuracy in federated learning.

accepted.question_text: Can one build an end-to-end cross-device differentially private federated learning protocol that remains robust to user availability changes and dropouts, computes a tight privacy guarantee from protocol-visible information alone, relies only on local participation decisions, and still achieves a strong privacy-utility trade-off in production systems?

evidence.quote: building an end-to-end protocol that works in production FL systems is still an important open problem.

accepted.question_text: How can implementations of differentially private federated learning be audited for correctness, including in black-box settings where the deploying organization does not expose source code or internal details of the implementation?

evidence.quote: What techniques can be used for testing FL-implementations for correctness?
what are the possibilities for black-box testing?

accepted.question_text: How should private federated learning algorithms be extended to streaming or time-evolving data, including how to update a learned model when new data arrive, how to maintain or refresh synthetic data privately over time, and how to support time-series queries when repeated sampling of the same individuals is limited by the federated setting?

evidence.quote: An open question is how these algorithmic techniques can be extended to the federated setting, to enable private federated learning on time series data or other dynamically evolving databases.
How should an analyst privately update an FL model in the presence of new data?

accepted.question_text: Even if model parameters are hidden inside trusted hardware or protected cryptographically, what additional safeguards are needed to stop attackers from reconstructing or stealing a deployed federated model through prediction-time access to its outputs at massive scale?

evidence.quote: It is an open question what additional protections would need to be put into place to protect from these kinds of issues in the context of a model residing on millions or billions of end user devices.

accepted.question_text: Can one construct a secure aggregation protocol for federated learning that is efficient at scale, robust to dropouts, does not rely on a semi-honest server, hides potentially revealing per-round aggregates, supports sparse vectors efficiently, and enforces that client inputs are well formed?

evidence.quote: It is an open question how to construct an efficient and robust secure aggregation protocol that addresses all of these challenges.

accepted.question_text: For distributed differential privacy based on shuffling or secure aggregation, what are the optimal trade-offs between privacy, communication, and accuracy, and what privacy-accounting methods are appropriate when the mechanisms use discrete noise rather than the Gaussian mechanisms common in centralized differential privacy?

evidence.quote: an important goal is nailing down the possible trade-offs between these parameters.
an important open problem is to derive privacy accounting techniques that are tailored to these discrete (and finite supported) noise distributions that are being considered for distributed DP.

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to do communication-efficient federated training of private submodels—such as sparse embedding updates or cluster-specific submodels—while keeping each client’s submodel choice hidden, co-optimizing private information retrieval with secure aggregation, and preserving sparsity even under distributed differential privacy?

evidence.quote: Is it possible to achieve communication-efficient sub-model federated learning while also keeping the client’s sub-model choice private?

It is also an open question whether private information retrieval (PIR) and secure aggregation might be co-optimized to achieve better communication efficiency than simply having each technology operate independently

It is an open question whether this tension can be resolved, i.e. whether there is a meaningful instantiation of distributed differential privacy that also maintains the sparsity of the model updates.

accepted.question_text: How can federated learning defend against poisoning attacks, backdoors, collusion, and Byzantine failures without direct access to raw client data, including whether redundancy-based defenses can be reconciled with low-communication constraints, whether data-sanitization or pruning ideas can be adapted privately, and how the power of data poisoning compares formally with direct model-update poisoning?

evidence.quote: One challenging open problem is reconciling redundancy-based defenses, which can increase communication costs, with federated learning, which aims to lower communication costs.

it is an open question whether data sanitization methods and network pruning methods can be used in federated settings without privacy loss, or whether or not defenses against data poisoning require new federated approaches.
One interesting line of study would be to quantify the gap between these two types of attacks, and relate this gap to the relative strength of an adversary operating under these attack models.

accepted.question_text: How should adversarial training and other defenses against inference-time evasion attacks be adapted to federated learning, especially when client data are non-IID, each example may be seen only a limited number of times, and generating adversarial examples on edge devices is computationally expensive?

evidence.quote: Adapting adversarial training methods to federated learning brings a host of open questions.
it is unclear how it performs in non-IID settings.

accepted.question_text: How can fairness be defined, measured, and improved in federated learning when sensitive attributes are unavailable, including scalable methods for equitable performance across unknown subpopulations and understanding the joint trade-offs among fairness, privacy, and robustness?

evidence.quote: approaches work for large-scale, high-dimensional data typical to federated settings is also an open problem
investigating and addressing these challenges is an open problem for future work.
An important open challenge is to develop a joint understanding of federated learning systems that are robust, private, and fair.
